div.div:
When the exit shutdown condition is set in an application specific ISR, the shutdown sequence is ended by issuing a software reset. The device could also be reset inside the ISR or through an external signal, however this implementation ensures compliance with the requirement that deep sleeping always ends in a device reset.
For simplicity, this condition is only checked after completing the above activities, meaning there is a minimum time required between entering the shutdown task manager and exiting it. If this is not acceptable by the application, the Restart Device Task can be scheduled directly in an ISR.
The software reset is issued in such a way that the Pre-startup Task Manager will report a non-error related software reset. If the software reset fails, it will continue to attempt the reset until another safety mechanism resets the device, such as the WDT timing out.

div.div:
Framework and application-specific interrupt handlers for any active interrupt sources. This should include the application-specific wake-up source(s) to request clearing the watchdogs and logic for determining whether to request exiting the shutdown state. See ad_shutdownArchIntExamples for examples.
This also includes the ISR for the CRCSCAN used by the optional Verify Flash Integrity Task, responsible for waking up the device when completing a scan or an error injection scan and reporting the result.
Since the SWDT and WDT are only cleared when the clear flag is set in an ISR, other interrupt sources can still wake the device and the Shutdown manager will automatically re-enter sleep. However, asynchronous wake-up events may introduce race conditions where the device returns to sleep without clearing the watchdogs or exiting shutdown. If the application spends too many clock cycles servicing ISRs instead of sleeping, the SWDT may eventually time out.
If the WDT is disabled and an exit is requested when waking up, clearing the watchdogs is unnecessary. However, if the device wakes up and goes back to sleep, the SWDT will eventually time out. In this case, each interrupt waking the device can request clearing the watchdogs.

div.div:
Reconfigures the WDT to a user defined timeout and ensures the SWDT can be cleared each time it wakes up from sleep by setting it to max open window and no closed window, given that the SWDT cannot be turned off, but does not count while the device is sleeping.
By default, all I/O pins are force floated to enter the Safe State. This can optionally be disabled if the application requires the application to produce an output during sleep. In this case, the unused pins can be manually floated in the Application Shutdown Task. Since the Error Controller is disabled in Standby and Power-Down sleep, the I/O heartbeat signal is also disabled during sleep. To avoid a glitching signal that occasionally toggles when waking up, the heartbeat should be manually disabled if force float is not used.
Since Standby and Power-Down sleep involves disabling clock sources, any active CFM or CFD will likely report an error. For this reason, all CFM and CFD modules are configured to be disabled by default in this task.
The Task also ensures global interrupts are enabled to be able to enter sleep and wake up.

div.div:
Optional user defined Task to ensure all application specific systems are suspended in a controlled manner before going into the Safe State. This could include disabling peripherals and external components or sending a message to other systems.
Task should also be responsible for enabling an optional application-specific periodic interrupt source to manage the watchdogs, the conditions for exiting the shutdown state and to disabling interrupts that should not wake up the device.

div.div:
In safe shutdown, the application is in a Safe State and the FDTI no longer applies. Thus the WDT can be set to a less strict timeout, as required by the application, as long as the period of the application-specific interrupt wakeup source is less than the WDT timeout. Alternatively, if the application has an external reset source, the WDT can be turned off, which simplifies the usage and reduces power consumption further.
In order to set a new WDT timeout, the WDT must be cleared within its current open window after re-configuration. The SWDT is used to ensure correct timing of this clear by waiting for a fixed duration larger than the closed window period.

div.div:
Optional Task to run CRCSCAN on the specified Flash memory sections to verify integrity of the program memory and report the result. This requires entering the Idle sleep mode until the scan of one section is complete, where a done signal interrupt wakes up the device. Should an unrelated interrupt source wake up the device, it will re-enter sleep in order to complete the scan. It is assumed that the scan time is much shorter than the WDT timeout and it will thus not clear the WDT. The SWDT will not count while sleeping.
The scan will always fail unless the expected CRC checksum is placed at the end of each Flash section under test by the user. For this reason, the Task is disabled by default.
This task can optionally also run the CRCSCAN error injection diagnostic before starting the scan.

div.div:
Enables either the Standby or Power-Down sleep mode, as configured by the application, and enters sleep to reduce power consumption while the application is not active.
In this state, most of the hardware safety mechanisms are disabled. This includes the ERRCTRL heartbeat signal.

div.div:
After waking up from an interrupt, check if a interrupt handler has set the flag to clear the SWDT and WDT or skip it before going back to sleep or exiting the shutdown sequence. If disabled, clearing the WDT has no effect.
In this simple implementation, there are no additional application tasks running nor is the Error Handler Notification Log checked since the application is inactive.
